newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Prospects seen positive for NZ 96/7 arable season.
newsitem.headline: Prospects seen positive for NZ 96/7 arable season.

text.p: New Zealand's arable farmers are positive about prospects for the 1996/97 season, Federated Farmers' Chairman Rab McDowell said on Monday.
Rab McDowell said in the farming lobby group's annual report that expectations were for increased planting and production in the season, and that arable farmers were in a positive mood.
"Decreasing world grain stock levels and increasing world-wide demand are driving up grain prices. This is accentuated by uncertain prospects for the USA harvest," he said.
"Although most of New Zealand's arable production is for the domestic market, it is not immune to world price trends. Expectations are firming markedly."
McDowell described the 1995/96 production season as "average to good".
Federated Farmers' dairy section chairman Malcolm Bailey said the outlook for 1996/97 was positive, although not as good as last season.
"Prices have eased, and background concerns remain about U.S. and European subsidised exports, despite continuing growth in dairy product demand," he said.
Bill Garland, chairman of the meat and wool section, said 1995/96 was a good season. Lamb prices slowly improved, although they were still not adequate.
"The BSE scare in the U.K. pushed up demand and prices for lamb in that market, which has helped," Garland said. He said end of season lamb prices in the South Island would be between NZ$38-40.
However, beef prices remained depressed in all markets because of world oversupply, and prospects for the next 18 months were for more of the same.
Garland said wool prices were a disaster.
However, he added, "unlike previous downturns, most farmers continue to put on fertiliser, which indicates that they are looking at longer term rather than short term survival".
